en: Vidyākaraśānti:
*Tarkasopāna* (Ts 275)
Homage to Mañjuśrī.
May the remembrance of Hevajra, who pierces ignorance like a boar in the lake of saṃsāra, abide for a long time within my heart.
1. Valid cognition (pramāṇa) is, by definition, the cause for the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful; this is briefly explained here.
Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge.
Contradiction is *visaṃvāda*; the absence of contradiction is *avisaṃvāda*.
That which possesses this [quality] is non-contradictory;
the meaning is that it is indeed consistent.
Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*), moreover, is the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) connected to the object that has been indicated.
Attainment (*prāpaṇa*) consists both in the state of being a bringer [of that action] and in the fitness for it.
In the case of immediate purposeful action, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possesses only the quality of being a bringer.

Even in the case of a mediated [cognition], there is both the quality of being an instigator and the quality of being a bringer-about; and this latter is nothing other than the quality of being a demonstrator.

Since the characteristic of an instrument (*karaṇadharma*) is taken to be the quality of being a demonstrator, those [cognitions] which apprehend what has already been apprehended are excluded as not being instruments; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
For this very reason, the teacher Dharmottara also said:
By that very [means] which first demonstrated the object, the person was set in motion and the object was attained; what further task remains for another?
Cognitions such as the perception of water in a mirage are excluded precisely because they are incapable of bringing about the purposeful action connected with the demonstrated object.
Furthermore, by the mention of "cognition" (*jñāna*), non-cognition (*ajñāna*) and the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are excluded.
And because [the subsequent cognition] apprehends what has already been apprehended by a suffix prescribed with the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*),
that knowledge which is capable of leading one to an object capable of the intended purposeful action, which possesses a previously unknown object, is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
2. That [means of valid cognition] is twofold:
perception and inference.
3. *Pratyakṣa* means that which has gone toward (*pratigata*) or rests upon (*āśrita*) the sense-organ (*akṣa*).
It is a compound formed according to the rule: "Words such as *ati* and others [form compounds] with a word in the second case when they have the sense of 'surpassing' (*krānta*) and so forth."
In compounds such as *prāpta-apanna*, *alaṅ-gati*, and *samāsa*, the gender of the subsequent member is prohibited.
By this rule, it is established that *pratyakṣaḥ pratyayaḥ* (direct perception as a cognition), *pratyakṣā buddhiḥ* (direct perception as an intellect),
and *pratyakṣaṃ jñānam* (direct perception as knowledge) are all valid.
Furthermore, the dependence of perception upon the senses is merely the cause for its etymological derivation;
its actual ground for application (pravṛttinimitta), however, is direct realization itself.
Consequently, it is established that any cognition whatsoever which directly realizes an object is denotable by the term "perception" (pratyakṣa).
That by which something is measured is *māna*.
Inference (*anumāna*) is the measurement that follows after the perception of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of its connection [with the probandum].
And this is obtained through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Therefore, that cognition which arises—having its object a thing beyond the senses—from one who has perceived a mark (*liṅga*) residing in a particular subject (*dharmin*) and who has remembered the relationship between the mark and the marked (*liṅgin*), is designated by the term "inference" (*anumāna*).
The word "and" (*ca*) conjoins perception and inference as being equal in authority;
for just as perception is a valid means of knowledge because it is invariably concomitant with the real object, so too is inference.
Likewise, inference also is a means of valid cognition because it is invariably concomitant with the object; thus it has been stated.
Since there is no [cognition] in the absence of an object, even in the case of perception there is the status of being a means of valid cognition;
for when that which has a nature connected [to the object] is its cause, both [perception and inference] are equal in this regard.

By this very demonstration of their equal strength, that which was asserted by the Mīmāṃsakas—that perception alone is the eldest among all means of valid cognition because inference and the rest are preceded by it—is also refuted;

for since all means of valid cognition depend upon their own causes for the attainment of their own existence (ātmasattālābhe), the conceptualization of a relationship between "eldest" and "younger" is not tenable. (Ts 77)
Thus, valid cognition is of only two kinds, distinguished as direct perception and inference.
5. By the statement that there are two [types of valid cognition], the conflicting views that there are three, four, five, or six are refuted.
For instance, for the followers of Bṛhaspati (the Cārvākas), perception alone is the valid cognition;
for the Sāṃkhyas, perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the valid cognitions.
The Naiyāyikas accept comparison as well;
the Prābhākaras accept presumptive testimony as well;
and the Grammarians hold that non-existence, perception, and verbal testimony are means of valid cognition.
6. Among these, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
That cognition which is devoid of conceptualization by way of being a conceptual construction and is non-erroneous—that alone is perception.
By this, [the following] which was stated by Uddyotakara [is refuted].
If by the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) perception itself is denoted,

how can it be "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha)? Or, if it is free from conceptual construction, how can that which is free from conceptual construction be expressed by this very word "perception"?
Furthermore, as Bhartṛhari has stated:
"Conceptualization is indeed cognition, and perception is also cognition.
By negating conceptual cognition within perceptual cognition, it is demonstrated that there exists another cognition distinct from that [conceptual] cognition.
The argument that "negations are preceded by prior affirmation" according to logical principle has been entirely refuted,
because what is intended here is the negation of identity (*tādātmya*).
For this very reason, it is explained as being "devoid of conceptual construction by virtue of its nature as non-conceptual.
If it is asked, "How is it that the absence of conceptual construction and error is established by direct perception?"—
it is because neither conceptual construction nor error possesses the direct apprehension of the form of the object.
For it is thus:
conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the cognition of an appearance that is capable of being associated with verbal expression;
verbal expression is the signifying word.

And that is a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*). That cognition in which there is an appearance capable of being conjoined with— that is, suitable for conjunction— with it— is "that which has an appearance capable of being conjoined with verbal expression" (*abhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsā*).

By the inclusion of the term "capable" (*yogya*), the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of a child who has not yet mastered linguistic conventions is encompassed. Although in that [conceptualization] there is no actual association with verbal expression, it is indeed capable of such association;
for the objective form appearing therein can be denoted by a word whose application of convention is subject to one's will.
If it is asked, "How then is the conceptual construction of an infant established? [the answer is:
because its effects, characterized by activity and so forth, are observed.
For instance, an infant proceeds toward the breast and so forth while avoiding the finger and such; as it has been said:
"In this world, all practical activity depends upon words;
even an infant understands that [activity] through the impressions deposited in the past."

Furthermore, in the case of an infant, one must infer a conceptual construction (kalpanā) revolving within the intellect, which is characterized by the forms and sounds of indistinct syllables; it is through this that the child later becomes skilled in grasping linguistic conventions.

Such [conceptualization] does not directly perceive the form of the object, because the form of the object does not appear to the intellect through the word in the same way it appears to the vision of one whose sense faculties are unengaged.
For that alone is the meaning of a word which appears in the verbal cognition;
the difference in apprehension arises from a difference in means, not from a difference in the object.
If it is argued that this is just as the same Devadatta is seen through a door and through a lattice window.
This is untenable.
Even if there is a difference in the means [of cognition], since that very same form is apprehended, how can there be a difference in comprehension?
Furthermore, things do not possess two forms characterized as clear and unclear, because of contradiction and because difference is based upon that [distinction between clear and unclear].
For this very reason, the example is also unestablished. As it has been said:
"The basis for cognitions is indeed that object itself, and nothing else;
how could a single entity possess a nature that appears in diverse forms?"
Thus, conceptualization (*kalpanā*) should grasp an object that is indeed capable of being expressed by joining it with a word;
and an expressible thing, when being directly realized, must be realized precisely as unjoined with a word.
This is established: conceptual construction does not have the direct perception of a real entity.

Even erroneous cognition—such as that produced by the impairment of cataracts, rapid spinning, traveling in a boat, or physical agitation—which deviates from the actual form of the object, how could it directly perceive an object existing in a different manner?
Because the manifestation of its own nature (svarūpa) is what is denoted by the term "direct perception" (sākṣātkaraṇa),
it is established that there is no direct perception of a real object even in the case of an illusion.

Consequently, since cognition directly perceives its object and is necessarily free from both conceptual construction (kalpanā) and illusion (vibhrama), it remains free from conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta).
In this context, by the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), inference is excluded;
by the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), cognitions such as that of a double moon are excluded.
Furthermore, by the principle that "what is intended for one purpose serves another," it should be understood that the misconceptions of others are also refuted.
For it has been said by the grammarians:
"There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
every cognition arises as if permeated by speech."

Thus, if all cognitions possessed a nature that follows after words (*śabdānugatarūpatva*), it would be impossible for any cognition whatsoever to directly perceive an object. Furthermore, how can one deny that perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), which is established by experience? For instance, at the time of conceptualizing a horse, there is still the experience of a cow.
That alone is non-conceptual perception;
nor does the conceptualization of "horse" itself apprehend the cow, because that [conceptualization] grasps its object only as associated with its own name.
Furthermore, no other conceptual construction (vikalpa) is perceived as an object of experience;
by this, the case of a conceptual construction of a cow or the like at a time when there is a conceptual construction of a horse or the like is also explained.
The same applies to the Mīmāṃsakas as well.
For there exists first a perceptual cognition that is non-conceptual,
resembling the consciousness of infants, the mute, and others, arising from the pure object itself.

"Furthermore, that cognition by which objects are subsequently determined through their properties such as genus and so forth is also accepted as being perception. By this, the status of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as perception is intended.

Even by the Naiyāyikas and others, through the statement "having the nature of a determinate cognition" (*vyavasāyātmakam*) and so forth, it has been asserted that only certainty (*niścaya*) is perception; this too is refuted by the very phrase "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍham*).
For if perception were of the nature of conceptual construction, its status as a direct intuition of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*) would be lost.
9. By the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), cognitions such as that of a yellow conch with respect to a white conch are also excluded;
for even though there is an error, there is an absence of non-contradiction regarding causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
Nor is it logical for that [cognition] to be an inference, because it does not arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, it is called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
But how is this [definition] excluded by the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) in the sense of being non-discrepant (*avisaṃvāda*)?
It is said:
Because it is impossible to obtain a purposeful action that corresponds to the form of the object as it was determined [by the cognition].

For if something were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) merely by being non-contradictory, then even the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*) and so forth would be a valid means of knowledge, since there is the possibility of correspondence with light and other such factors.
10. That direct perception is fourfold:
sensory cognition, mental cognition, self-reflexive awareness, and the cognition of yogins.

11. Sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) is the knowledge based upon the sense faculties—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. Mental cognition (*mānasa*) is that which is produced by sensory cognition acting as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), together with a subsequent moment of the same kind that is derived from its own object; it is so called because it relies solely upon the mind. Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is that form by which all minds and mental factors are experienced by themselves.
Yoga is tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*prajñā*); those who possess these are *yogins*.
Their cognition—arising from the culmination of the intensification of meditation upon an object established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—is *yogic cognition*.
By explaining the fourfold classification [of perception], those who have imagined the sense faculty itself to be the seer in the case of mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) [are refuted].
The faults [previously] raised are as follows: self-awareness is not admitted, and since yogis themselves do not exist, how could there be their cognition? Thus, all those [objections] are refuted.

12. For instance, the Vaibhāṣikas [argue] that since cognition (*jñāna*) is non-obstructive (*apratigha*), if it were the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), it would perceive even what is obstructed; therefore, they postulate the sense faculty (*indriya*) as the seer.
But this is not tenable.

For if cognition perceives an object by going to it, then one could rightly say that it would perceive even what is obstructed, because there would be no obstacle to its movement. However, [cognition does not go]. Thus, the postulation is incorrect.

However, it is said that an object is apprehended by a cognition insofar as that cognition arises with the form of that object; yet an object situated in an inaccessible location does not possess a form identical to that [cognition].
Therefore, how could there be an apprehension of it by that [cognition]?
Furthermore,
if the sense faculty were the seer, then there would be no apprehension of an object obstructed by glass or similar materials,
because of the established tenet that the ten material elements are characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*).
How is it stated in the Āgama: "Form is grasped by the eye"? This designation is metaphorical.

13. Furthermore, as Kumārila and others have stated: "If mental cognition apprehends an object already apprehended by sensory cognition, then it lacks validity because it apprehends what has already been apprehended."
Furthermore, [the objection that] it would then perceive an object not grasped by sensory cognition,
which would lead to the fault of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth—

that too is refuted by the very fact that [the cognition] is produced by a sensory cognition accompanied by a moment of the same kind that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of its own objective moment.
For instance, mental cognition (mānasa) perceives the momentary state that is the effect of the object of sensory cognition;
yet sensory cognition does not exist for those who are blind and so forth.
Therefore, how could there be the fault of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and others?
Nor does it involve grasping what has already been grasped,
because it grasps the momentary state that arises as the effect of the object of sensory cognition.
And this is accepted as mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) when the activity of the eye and other senses has ceased.
Furthermore, when this [mind] is active, if that which is perceptual is not born of the senses, what else could be born of the senses?
Nor should one suspect that this contradicts experience because there is no perception of form for one with eyes closed;
for it is difficult to discern [the mind's activity] due to its occurring for only a single moment.
If it is asked, "For what purpose, then, has this been introduced? it is said in reply:
It is to demonstrate that if that which is described as mental in our established doctrine (siddhānta) were indeed characterized in such a way, then no fault alleged by others would apply.
Furthermore, the claim made by others that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not admitted regarding the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) is also untenable.
For it is not the case that the manifestation of the mind and mental factors does not exist at all,
since such manifestation is established through the experience of all living beings.
Nor is it logical for these [cognitions] to be illuminated by another.

For first of all, it is untenable that a subsequent [cognition] existing at the same time [as the object] could be its illuminator, because there is no mutual assistance. Furthermore, even one existing at a different time cannot be an illuminator, because the thing to be illuminated would then be non-existent.
Therefore, just as a lamp illuminates itself because its nature is to illuminate, so too does cognition.
If it is objected that even a lamp is illuminated by the eye, we reply: no, for it was cited as an example precisely because it does not depend on an illuminator of its own kind.
15. Furthermore, if cognition does not cognize itself, then, since it would not be perceptible by itself, the manifestation of objects would likewise not be perceptible. Here is the formal argument:
That which has an unmanifest manifestation is not manifest;

for example, like something that is at some time and in some way unmanifestly manifested. And since an object such as a jar is unmanifestly manifested when it is beyond the reach of cognition, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-perception of the pervader.
In this case, manifestness (vyaktatva) is the property to be negated;
its pervader is the state of being both manifest and unmanifest;
and that [pervader] is not perceived here.
If it is argued that this reason— namely, that the manifestation of a cognition occurs through another cognition— is unestablished (*asiddha*),
we say no; for it is established at the time when cognitions of jars and other such objects arise.
Moreover, even for you, not every cognition is known by a cognition that inheres in the same object,
because in the absence of a desire to know, that [subsequent cognition] does not arise,
just as in the case of a cognition whose object is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*).
Consequently, that which is to be disregarded would itself result in being unmanifest, because its manifestation is unmanifest.
Furthermore, it must be explained how knowledge itself is manifested by knowledge;
for if it were said to be established by another cognition, the same would apply there as well, resulting in an infinite regress.
Nor is this [reason] inconclusive due to its exclusion from the counter-example being doubtful;

for if even that which has unmanifest manifestation were the object of the conventional usage "manifest," then the cognition residing in another person, though unmanifest, would likewise be conventionally designated as "manifest" at the very time its own cognition arises, just like [a cognition] in one's own case.
Thus, this linguistic convention regarding the manifest is all-pervasive by virtue of its being both manifest and non-manifest.
And once the relationship of pervaded and pervader is established, the non-perception of the pervader is conclusive.
Nor is there any contradiction in an action operating upon itself.
When self-awareness is precisely origination itself, distinguished from insentient objects,
it was stated by the venerable teacher Śāntarakṣita:
Consciousness arises as something distinct from insentient forms;
this very quality of being non-insentient is its self-awareness.
The meaning of the term "self-cognition" (svasaṃvit) has also been shown by them [the masters] as follows:
"In the cognition of its own nature, it does not depend on another cognizer, nor is there anything that remains uncognized; this is the meaning of self-cognition. Thus.
17. As for what was said—that yogins themselves do not exist, so how could they possess knowledge?—that is without substance.
For cultivation (bhāvanā), whether its object is a real thing or otherwise, when it reaches the limit of its intensification, produces a cognition with an extremely clear apprehended form.

For instance, those whose mental states are overwhelmed by grief and the like become possessed of clearly revolving appearances upon the completion of their meditation on [objects such as] a son and so forth.

In that context, that which arises from the culmination of the intensification of meditation on an object established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which grasps the extremely clear form of the meditated object like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand—that is the yogic direct perception (*yogipratyakṣa*).
As it has been said:
That non-conceptual knowledge which, through the power of cultivation, manifests clearly— just as in the case of fear and the like—
and is non-erroneous, is perception.
18. Its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That which is perceived by this fourfold [perception] in its unique, non-common form is the object.
By this, the attribution of a universal as the object of perception is refuted.
That object, through whose presence or absence there is a difference in the manifestation of cognition, is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"Presence" of that object which is the domain of cognition means its location in a suitable place;
"absence" means its total non-existence in a suitable place.

That which, through those two, distinguishes the appearance of cognition from the form of the apprehended object by way of its arising and non-arising—that is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Any other [object] is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); that is the object of inference (*anumāna*).
Whatever is common to others, distinct from this particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is the object of inference.
That very perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
Because it consists in the cognition of the object, that very perceptual knowledge which was just mentioned is itself the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Cognition of the object" means its comprehension;
[it is the fruit] because it has that as its nature.
If that very cognition is not accepted as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), then there would be a difference in the objects of the means of valid cognition and its fruit;
and this is not tenable,
for when an axe or similar tool reaches a *khadira* tree, the cutting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree.

20. Its validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in its conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*), because it is by virtue of that [conformity] that the cognition of the object is established. In this context, whatever object from which a consciousness arises, the [consciousness] becomes similar in form to that [object].
Because it is impossible to know an object through a cognition that does not possess its form;
for consciousness arises with the nature of mere awareness alone.
In that case, there would be no determination of specific objects, such as "this is the cognition of blue" or "this is the cognition of yellow."
For it is of the same nature whether [the object] be blue or yellow.
However, when there is a similarity of form with the object, that cognition which conforms to the form of a particular thing is the awareness of that very thing and not of anything else.
And this similarity of form is the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is the most effective instrument for establishing the definite cognition of a specific object.
And this should not be thought:
"How can there be no difference between the probandum and the probans?
For in this case, the relationship of probandum and probans does not exist by way of the relationship of produced and producer.
And this is logically consistent even for a single entity by way of the relationship between the established and the establisher; nor is there any contradiction with worldly convention,
for the world also sometimes speaks of a single thing, such as a bow, in terms of its agency and so forth.
For instance, speakers say:
"He pierces with a bow," or "He pierces by means of a bow."

By the statement, "Having released an arrow from the bow, one pierces [the target]," the misconception regarding the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*)— namely, that each preceding cognition is the instrument and each subsequent one is the result— is refuted.
In the *Tarkasopāna*, the first chapter, the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is concluded.
1. Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (svārtha) and for others (parārtha). That which is for oneself is "for oneself," by means of which one understands for oneself.
This is for the sake of another (*parārtha*). That by which one causes another to understand [the object] is [inference for others].

In that regard, the knowledge regarding the inferable (*anumeya*) arising from a mark possessing the three characteristics—that is, the knowledge having the inferable as its object which arises from a mark endowed with the three forms—is inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
The inclusion of the three characteristics is for the purpose of excluding [reasons] that possess only one or two characteristics respectively.
Among these, a reason possessing only a single characteristic is not valid;
for example: "Sound is eternal because it is produced."

"Because of having form" and "because of being immeasurable" refer, respectively, to presence in the subject (*anumeya*), presence in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). (Ts 286)
There is only the mere [logical mark], for it possesses two forms, just as sound is impermanent because it is incorporeal and because it is audible.
"And because of being visible" [is stated] because,
respectively, there is an absence of mere existence in the subject (*anumeya*), existence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and non-existence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*).
This was stated by the venerable Teacher:
Nor is an object established in reality by means of a mark that has a single, double, or twofold form.
"Sound is eternal because it is produced; [it is] imperceptible because it is corporeal;
[it is] non-eternal because it is incorporeal and inaudible, and because it is visible.
(3) By the inclusion of the term "inferable" (*anumeya*), objects that are directly perceived (*aparokṣa*) are excluded.

The establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its result (phala) here is also like that of perception. Just as in perception it was stated that the conformity (sārūpya) of the cognition itself with the blue object and so forth is the means of valid cognition, and the cognition of the blue object and so forth is the result, so too here, the form of fire and so forth is the means of valid cognition, and the nature of the conceptualization (vikalpana) of fire and so forth is the result. 4. The logical mark (liṅga) has three characteristics (rūpa).

"Certainty of existence only in the inferable" means that the existence of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the inferable—whose definition will be stated later—is ascertained as having a single form. Among these, by the word "existence," the unestablished (*asiddha*) reason is excluded;
for example, [the argument] "Sound is eternal."
Regarding the phrase "because of being visible":
by the use of the particle *eva*, the reason that is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is excluded;
for example, [the argument] "trees are sentient because they sleep."
Among the trees taken as the subject of the argument, sleep characterized by the closing of leaves is not established even in one part [of the subject];
for not all trees possess the closing of leaves at night,
but only some.
By placing the particle *eva* (only) after the word "of the subject" (*sattva*), the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is excluded;
otherwise, for instance, "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) would itself become a valid reason in the argument "it is impermanent because it is audible.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*), reasons such as the "doubtful-unestablished" (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*) are excluded.
Just as a mass of elements, when suspected of being steam or the like, is employed for the purpose of establishing fire;
existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*)— where the similar class has the definition to be stated later— is the second characteristic, which is determined existence in that very [class].
Here too, by the inclusion of the term "sentient being" (*sattva*), the contradictory [reason] is excluded, just as in the case: "It is eternal, because it is produced.
This is because that very [reason] does not exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
By the word "only" (eva), the common inconclusive [reason] is excluded;
for example, "sound is eternal because it is knowable.
For that reason does not reside in the similar class alone, but rather in both [the similar and dissimilar classes].

By the word "existence" (*sattva*) preceded by the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*), the status of being a logical reason (*hetu*) is stated even for that which exists in only some members of the similar class (*sapakṣa*);
for example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced immediately after an effort.
And by the repeated use of the word "ascertained" (*niścita*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason whose positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful is excluded.
For example: "Someone is omniscient because they are a speaker.

For the property of being a speaker is doubtful in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), namely the omniscient person, while its absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) is certain; thus this [fallacy] also applies here.
The dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) is defined by what will be stated below.
In that case, non-existence itself is determined as the third form [of the reason]. By the mention of "non-existence" therein, the contradictory [reason] is excluded;
for the contradictory exists in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
By the word "only" (eva), there is the exclusion of a common [reason] that occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
For example: "Sound is produced immediately after effort, because it is impermanent.

For when "being produced immediately after effort" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the property of impermanence exists in only a portion of the dissimilar instances, such as lightning and the like.
It does not exist in space and so forth;
therefore, it is excluded by means of this restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*).
If the restriction were placed before the word "non-existence" (*asattva*), the meaning would be as follows:
That which does not exist even in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is a [valid] reason (*hetu*).
And likewise, the property of "being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) does not exist even in the similar class (*sapakṣa*);
therefore, it would not be a reason.
Therefore, it was not established previously.
By the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*), the case where the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful is rejected;
for example: "Devadatta’s son is dark-skinned because he is his son, like the sons currently observed."
(Ts 288) But surely, when it is stated that "it exists in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*), it is understood that it exists *only* in the similar class; so what is the purpose of mentioning both?
True.

However, either the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) must be employed as something possessing necessary restriction (*niyamavat*), so that when the positive concomitance is employed, there is a comprehension of the positive concomitance.
Therefore, since the employment of both together in a single application should not be made, the employment of both has been made here for the purpose of instruction.
5. Here, the "object of inference" (*anumeya*) is the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific property is desired to be known.

In this context, while the definition of the probans (hetu) is to be ascertained, the phrase "grasping the specific feature sought to be known" indicates merely the state of having an unknown specific feature; for otherwise, the cognition of fire and so forth on a mountain peak and such places— which arises from the mere perception of smoke and so forth by one who possesses the recollection of pervasion and is searching for fire— would not be included.

A *sapakṣa* (similar instance) is an object that is similar by way of the commonality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Whatever object is similar—that is, like—the subject (*pakṣa*), that is called a *sapakṣa*. It is distinguished by the word "similar" through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*); it is a "similar side," hence a *sapakṣa*.
And that substitution of the word *samāna* occurs by means of a rule-split (*yogavibhāga*).
However, one should not [interpret] it as "that which has a similar side" (*samānaḥ pakṣo 'sya*);
for in that case, the similarity of the *sapakṣa* with the *pakṣa* would not be established.
Furthermore, it would be established that the subject itself possesses similarity to the similar instance (sapakṣa);
but this is not the case, because the similar instance is unestablished.
For that definition is indeed being formulated right now.

And "similarity" consists in the commonality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). 7. The non-similar instance (*asapakṣa*) is that which is other than the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), its opposite, and its absence.
The logical marks (liṅga) are exactly three, possessing the three characteristics:
non-perception (anupalabdhi), essential nature (svabhāva), and effect (kārya).
Among these, the non-perception of that which is to be negated and which meets the conditions for perceptibility is the means of establishing the conventional usage of its absence.

The fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) consists in the completeness of all other conditions for apprehension and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). That nature which, when other conditions for apprehension are present, becomes directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) itself [is that specific nature].

An object that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) means "visible. Even if such an object does not exist here, the phrase "it would be visible if it were present" refers to the domain of possibility; thus, it is called "having reached the conditions for apprehension."
The non-perception of that [object] establishes the conventional usage of its non-existence.
The inclusion of qualifiers is for the purpose of excluding other conditions that are remote in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, non-perception here is not mere negation, because such negation is not itself established, and even if it were established, it would not be a constituent part [of the proof].
Rather, it is simply the perception of another entity; moreover, this is not the perception of just any entity whatsoever,
but specifically of that which implies the absence of the object to be negated.
But it does not refer to that which is associated with the same single cognition.

For if the perception of another object associated with the same single cognition were the defining characteristic of non-perception, then how could the absence of Devadatta himself be established here by the perception of [another] Devadatta outside?
For in that case, there is no perception of another object associated with the same single cognition.

8. Furthermore, this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is of two kinds according to whether it is a property of the object (*karman*) or the subject (*kartṛ*). In that regard, when non-apprehension is a property of the object, it is the ground as distinct from the jar; but when it is a property of the subject, it is the cognition based upon that [ground].
In this regard, that absence of the jar is simply the very nature of the ground; therefore, it is indeed apprehended by the cognition that perceives the ground.
Consequently, this non-apprehension establishes the conventional usage of "non-existence" only for one who is deluded, since for one who is not deluded, it is established by perception itself.

However, non-perception of the cause and the other [types of non-apprehension], when operating upon an imperceptible object, certainly establish non-existence. And this [non-perception] is a means of cognition regarding the present time, and regarding the past time as well, provided there is no lapse of memory or mental attention.
Therefore: "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived."
It is possible to determine that "there was no jar here because it was not perceived," but one cannot [determine] that "there will be no jar here because it will not be perceived."
Because that which has not yet come into being possesses an uncertain nature.
9. And this [non-perception] is of many kinds due to the difference in its application. Among these:
1) non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). For example: "There is no smoke here, because that which has reached the conditions for perception is not perceived."
For smoke is indeed that which is to be negated; the non-perception of its intrinsic nature is [the first type].
2) Non-perception of the cause:
as in "there is no smoke here because of the absence of fire."
For fire is the cause of smoke, which is what is to be negated; here, there is a non-perception of that [fire].
3) Non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is, for example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because of the absence of trees.
For the *śiṃśapā* is what is to be negated, and the tree is its pervader; there is a non-perception of that [tree].
4) Non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*): for example, "There are no causes of smoke here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of the absence of smoke.
Smoke is the effect of the causes of smoke which are to be negated, and its non-perception occurs here.
5) Perception of that which is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*).
For example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire.
Here, fire is incompatible with the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the sensation of cold, which is the object to be negated, and fire is perceived here.

6) Perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*): For example, "He does not possess specific states such as horripilation, because of the presence of a particular fire."
Cold is the cause of the specific qualities to be negated, such as horripilation and the like; its opposite is a specific kind of fire, and that [fire] is perceived here.

7) Perception of the Opposite of the Pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*): for example, "there is no sensation of frost here, because of fire. Cold is the pervader of the sensation of frost to be negated; its opposite is fire, and that [fire] is perceived here.
8) Perception of what is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*): for example, "There are no causes of cold here with unimpeded capacity, because of fire.
Cold is the effect of the causes of cold which are to be negated; fire is incompatible with that [cold], and its perception occurs here.

9) Perception of what is pervaded by that which is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*): for example, "There is no fire here, because of the sensation of frost. The essential nature of the fire to be negated is heat; that which is contradictory to it is coldness; the sensation of frost is pervaded by that [coldness], and its perception occurs here.
10) Perception of what is pervaded by that which is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*): for example, "There is no smoke here, because of the sensation of frost."

For smoke, which is the object to be negated, has fire as its cause; that which is contrary to it is cold. Frost-touch is pervaded by that [cold], and here there is the perception of it. (11) Perception of what is pervaded by the contrary of the pervader is, for example: "This is not eternal, because it performs its function only at certain times. For eternity, which is the object to be negated, has "lack of variation" (*niratiśayatva*) as its pervader; that which is contrary to it is "possessing variation" (*sātiśayatva*). Performing its function only at certain times is pervaded by that [possessing variation], and here there is the perception of it.

12) Perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the effect (*kāryaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), as in: "There are no causes of fire here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of the sensation of frost. For the effect of the causes of fire—which are the objects of negation—is fire; that which is contradictory to it is cold; the sensation of frost is pervaded by that [cold]; and its perception occurs here. 13) Perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), as for example:
"There is no cold touch here because of smoke.
For fire is the contradictory of the cold touch which is to be negated; smoke is its effect, and its perception occurs here.

14) Perception of the effect of that which is contradictory to the cause is, for example: "This place does not contain a person characterized by specific symptoms such as horripilation, because of smoke."

Cold is the cause of the specific states to be negated, such as horripilation and the like; fire is its opposite; smoke is the effect of that [fire]; and here, there is the perception of that [smoke]. (Ts 292) 15) An example of the perception of the effect of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is as follows:
"Because there is smoke here, there is no touch of frost.

In this case, coldness is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the touch of frost, which is the object of negation; fire is its opposite (*viruddha*); and smoke is the effect (*kārya*) of that [fire], and its perception occurs here.

16) The perception of the effect of something incompatible with an effect (*kāryaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is, for example: "The causes of cold, whose capacities are unimpeded, do not exist here, because of smoke."
Cold is the effect of those causes of cold which are to be negated; fire is the opposite of that [cold]; smoke is the effect of that [fire]; and its [smoke's] perception occurs here.
10. All these fifteen applications of non-apprehension, beginning with the non-apprehension of the cause, are included within the non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Although there is a distinction in their application due to the affirmation or negation of other things (*arthāntara*) through an indirect sequence, they reach inclusion within the non-apprehension of the essential nature by way of identity (*tādātmya*).
This is what is meant:
first of all, the nature of non-apprehension is common to all [types of evidence];
likewise, even in cases such as the apprehension of something incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), the nature of non-apprehension is indeed present.
That perception which implies the non-existence of something is the non-perception of that thing, because it possesses the definition of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
For instance, this perception of fire implies the absence of cold.
[Objection: Let it be non-perception; but how can there be "visibility" (*dṛśyatā*) in that case?
It is said:
[the reason is] "non-perception despite being perceptible.
For if the cold touch were perceptible, then fire—which is pervaded by the absence of that [cold touch]—would certainly exclude its perception.

Thus, every non-apprehension that establishes non-existence, by the force of pervasion, contradicts the apprehension of a perceptible object; therefore, it is by implication a non-apprehension of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*),
not directly.

However, in that case where the perceptibility of the object to be negated is established for that very cognizer at that very time, non-perception of the perceptible is itself its specific characteristic;
thus, this is the direct non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
As for what is further stated by others:

Even though the present non-perception of the perceptible does not exist at the time of contradiction and so forth, it was precisely that [present non-perception] which served as the basis for the cognition of the [non-existent] entity.

Therefore, because the perception of what is contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and other such [reasons] are preceded by the non-perception of the perceptible, they are included within the non-perception of the perceptible.

Furthermore, since the present non-perception of the perceptible is absent [at those times], there is a distinction between the non-perception of its own essential nature and the other types of non-perception.

12. Furthermore, although some describe the perception of what is contradictory to intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth as being essentially non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*)—since they are forms of inference based on inference (anumitānumāna)—in that one perceives a specific color of fire from a distance and infers a specific hot touch pervading that location, and from that, the cognition of the absence of cold touch arises;
nevertheless, because it does not arise directly from the non-perception of the perceptible, it is taught as distinct from the non-perception of the perceptible.

For this very reason, this is merely an inference based on an inference (anumitānumāna); it is called a single inference only because, due to extreme familiarity, such a cognition arises instantaneously.

In reality, however, this consists of multiple inferences. This same principle should be understood to apply elsewhere as well, such as in the case of the perception of something incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalambha) and so forth; thus, neither of these two [definitions] provides satisfaction to the mind.
13. An essential nature (*svabhāva*) is a reason (*hetu*) for a property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) that exists solely by virtue of its own existence.

That which exists in dependence upon the existence of the reason itself, and does not depend on anything other than the existence of the reason, is the essential nature with respect to that which is to be proven. This is the reason.
And by this qualification, the inclusion of that effect which arises from the final cause is accomplished;
for even that is indeed its very nature,
because it comes into being merely through the existence of that [cause].
By the principle that "even what is established for one purpose serves another purpose," the opponent's misconception is also refuted;

for opponents maintain that a property such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva), even if it occurs at a later time, constitutes the essential nature (svabhāva), just as in the argument: "This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*."
The subject under discussion is that a reason (*hetu*) is that which is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvin*) with as many intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) as there are in the effect.
When the cause is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason consists of precisely those intrinsic natures with which it is inseparably connected;
for example, "there is fire here, because of smoke."
14. And these three types of logical marks (liṅga) exist due to the difference in what is to be proven (sādhya).
For the determination of a logical mark depends upon that which is to be proven;
and that which is to be proven is either an affirmation or a negation, because these two are characterized by the mutual exclusion of their respective definitions.
Affirmation (vidhi) is also twofold, due to the distinction between that which is not a different object and that which is a different object.

Among these, when what is to be understood is not a different object, it is a reason of essential nature (svabhāvahetu); but when what is to be understood is a different object, it is an effect (kārya). These two are the means of proof for affirmation.

For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one object (*artha*) causes another object to be known. An essential connection is the state of having an essentially connected nature.
This is because, when an essential connection exists, the meaning of the probans (*sādhanārtha*) causes the meaning of the probandum (*sādhyārtha*) to be known.
Therefore, it is only these two that possess the status of being means of proof for a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

But is it not the case that even without an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), there is the cognition of the blooming of night-lilies and the swelling of the ocean from the rising of the moon;
and the cognition of shadow on the opposite side from the presence of sunlight?
Furthermore, the rising of Rohiṇī and the other stars is perceived immediately after the rising of Kṛttikā and the others;

how then can it be said that "an object makes another object known" when there is an essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha)? For that which is not so connected lacks the necessity of non-deviation from it.
The word "that" (*tad*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is not connected with that [nature] is "unconnected with it.

Whatever is not connected by way of its intrinsic nature to something else necessarily does not fail to deviate from that object which is unconnected; thus, there is no rule of non-deviation between those two.
The cognition of the rising of the ocean [tide] from the rising of the moon and so forth arises solely from inference (*anumāna*).
For instance, there is an inference here of the very property of the cause (*hetudharma*) in cases where the blooming of lotuses and the like occur at the same time.
This being so, this is the establishment of the cause from the effect (*kāryāt kāraṇasiddhiḥ*).
And that very specific wind which is the cause for the rising of Kṛttikā and the other lunar mansions is indeed, through a continuous series, the cause for the rising of Rohiṇī and the others;
since the cognition of the effect arises from the cognition of the nature of the cause,
it is the same here as well.
Where there is non-deviation, there an invariable connection (pratibandha) is to be inferred; and that invariable connection of the mark (liṅga) with the object to be proven (sādhya) exists,
in reality, because of identity (tadātmya) and because of origination from that (tadutpatti).
Because that which does not possess that nature and that which is not produced from it lack an essential connection (*apratibaddhasvabhāvatva*) with respect to it;
and since those two— identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from it (*tadutpatti*)— exist only in the case of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*),
the establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) occurs through these two alone.
The establishment of a negation, however, proceeds from non-apprehension exactly as previously described.
Now, one might ask: what is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the case of non-apprehension?
For it is only a reason that is connected [to its probandum] which is a prover.
For it has just been stated:
"When there is an essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha), one object makes another object known.
In that regard, in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi), the connection consists in identity (tādātmya).
For in that case, what is being established is the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence; and since this fitness is nothing other than the very nature of the fit object,
the relationship between the signifier and the signified in cases such as the non-perception of the cause is based upon a fundamental necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

In the case of the perception of the incompatible (*viruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth, however, because [the object] is the effect of a specific location devoid of that [other thing] and so on, the basis for the production of such a fire and the like is precisely that [causal relation].
The second chapter, on inference for oneself, in the *Tarkasopāna*.
1. Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*).

That which was previously described as the logical mark with its three characteristics—the speech that makes it manifest is "inference for the sake of others," because the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause.

This is due to the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*), that is, the superimposition (*samāropa*), of the effect, namely inference, onto its cause, the logical mark possessing the three characteristics.
Just as the water in a reed-thicket causes a foot disease;
that [example] is of two kinds due to the difference in application: the one possessing similarity (*sādharmyavat*).
And because it is stated by way of dissimilarity.
2. That which possesses a common property is *sadharmā*. The state of being that is *sādharmya*.
It is the similarity between the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), produced by the reason (*hetu*).

That which has a dissimilar property is *vidharmā*; its state is *vaidharmya*. It is the dissimilarity between the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), produced by the reason (*hetu*). That syllogism whose expressed content is similarity is "possessing similarity" (*sādharmyavat*).
And that which has dissimilarity as its subject matter is "possessing dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyavat*).

Now, in a proof-statement possessing similarity (*sādharmyavat*), there is no negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); and in one possessing dissimilarity, there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*). How, then, could the communication of the three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) constitute inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*)?
This is not a fault;
for even in an argument formulated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is understood by implication,
because in its absence, it would be impossible for the reason (*hetu*) to be concomitant with the probandum (*sādhya*).

In a formal argument (prayoga) endowed with a subject matter characterized by similarity (sādharmya), the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is understood through implication; therefore, there is the statement of the three-fold mark (trirūpaliṅga).

This is because, when that negative concomitance is determined by the intellect, there is an absence of a positive concomitance (anvaya) of the reason (hetu) with the probandum (sādhya) as determined by the intellect.
(3) Likewise, there is also the comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya*);
for if that [dissimilar instance] were absent, the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) would remain unestablished.

"So be it. Just as in the case of the positive statement (*anvaya-vākya*), so too in the application by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there is an understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) even though it is not explicitly stated;

for if that positive concomitance were not grasped by the intellect, one could not determine the absence of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), since [the absence] would be unestablished.

Therefore, by means of a single statement—whether formulated by way of positive concomitance or by way of negative concomitance—the existence or non-existence of the mark (*liṅga*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is made known; thus, the employment of two statements is not necessary.

4. In that regard, the formal argument based on non-apprehension and similarity is as follows: whatever, being capable of being perceived, is not perceived in a certain place, is the object of the conventional designation of "non-existent" in that place;
for example, a horn on the head of a hare.
And a jar, though capable of being perceived, is not perceived in a particular location.

In this context, the similarity to be expressed is that which is established by the non-apprehension of the object of negation—characterized by its fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension—in both the subject of the example, the hare’s head, and the subject of the thesis, the specific location.
Likewise is the formulation of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*):
"Whatever exists is all impermanent, like a pot; and sound exists."
The application [of the reason] is to the pure intrinsic nature,
because mere existence does not depend on any substratum;
that which possesses origination is impermanent.

Just as in the case of "the pot," and since happiness possesses origination, this is an example of a non-distinct qualification; for origination is indeed the acquisition of one's own nature (*svarūpa*).
And that [property] is in fact the very essence of the entity itself; it is merely presented as if distinct through conceptual construction.
For instance, in the case of the qualification "distinct," one says: "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a pot; and sound is produced.
Indeed, an entity is called "produced" (kṛtaka) when its own nature is brought to completion through the operation of another factor upon which it depends.
In this way, [the properties] such as being differentiated by the differentiation of conditions are to be understood.
For here, what is to be expressed is the similarity between the subjects of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and the subjects of the examples (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) as produced by the cause.
All these proving-properties (*sādhanadharma*) [are to be applied] according to their respective [contexts]. (Ts 298)

By means of the valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), one must understand that only the property which is established as being concomitant with the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) is [the reason]; for in reality, that [property] alone has that [probandum] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
since it is impossible for that which is not established when the [latter] is established to have that as its intrinsic nature.
Because the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference.
6. The formal argument based on the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) with similarity (*sādharmya*):
Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen;
and there is smoke here.

In this context, what must be stated is the similarity between the locus of the example (the kitchen) and the specific locus of the subject of the thesis (the particular place), which is produced by the cause that is smoke.

Here too, once the relationship of cause and effect has been established through three non-perceptions and two perceptions, when the cause is to be proven, the "effect-reason" (kāryahetu) should be stated.
This is the formulation based on dissimilarity (vaidharmya) regarding non-perception.
Whatever exists and meets the conditions for perception is necessarily perceived,
just as a particular instance of blue is perceived.
Yet, in this case, there is no perception of the jar, even though it meets the conditions for perception.

For here, the dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*) between the subject of the example—the particular blue thing—and the subject of the thesis—the location—is to be stated as being produced by the reason known as the non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), which is to be negated.

Applications of the essential nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) possessing negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*): Where there is no impermanence, there is no existence at all, as in the case of a sky-flower;
yet sound exists.
If impermanence were absent, there would be no possession of origination anywhere, as in the case of space;
yet pleasure possesses origination.
If impermanence were absent, there would be no quality of being produced anywhere, as in the case of a tortoise’s hair.

And in the case of "sound is produced," what is to be expressed here is the dissimilarity between the subject of the example and the subject of the thesis (the probandum) as established by the reason.
8. An application of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*):
"Where there is no fire, smoke does not exist at all, as in a great lake;
yet, here there is smoke."

In this context, what is to be expressed is the dissimilarity between the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) and the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) as produced by the reason (*hetu*).

9. Since inference for the sake of others is defined as the statement of a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics, it follows by implication that the statement of the thesis (pakṣa) and so forth is not called inference.
In this regard, the proposition (pratijñā) is not a direct means of proof, because the object [to be proven] is understood through the meaning [of the reason] alone.
For it is the object itself that causes another object to be understood through a necessary connection;
not the verbal expression, because the reverse is the case.
This does not occur even through a mediated succession.
Because it is the probandum itself that is being expressed.

If it is argued that the thesis (*pratijñā*), although not a formal member [of the syllogism], is employed—just like the example—for the purpose of demonstrating the specific characteristics of the property to be proven and the proving property, [we reply: no;
for in that case, statements such as "admission" (*anujñā*) and so forth would also have to be employed.
For without those [auxiliaries], the operation of the means of proof is not possible;
even the presentation of the object [of inference] would be fruitless,
since the cognition of the probandum occurs even without that.

For instance, when one employs merely this much—"whatever is produced is all impermanent, and sound is produced"—the cognition that "sound is impermanent" indeed arises even without the statement of a proposition (*pratijñā*).
[Objection: But if the statement of the proposition is absent, how can there be the determination of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and so forth?
For instance, a similar class is an object that is similar by virtue of possessing the general property of the probandum (*sādhyadharma*).
And it is said that the non-concordant set (*asapakṣa*) is characterized by the absence of that [the property to be proved].
For if there were no statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), the three-fold character (*trairūpya*)—which is based on its dependence upon the subject (*pakṣa*)—would not exist.
This is incorrect.
For indeed, everything is accomplished even without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Furthermore, since the meaning of the application (*upanaya*) has already been indicated by the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it serves no purpose whatsoever if it were to precede that [statement].
In a formulation where pervasion (*vyāpti*) comes first, its meaning is established from the statement of the property of the subject alone; so what is the use of this *upanaya*?
The conclusion (nigamana) is also not an undesirable member of the syllogistic argument (sādhana-vākya).
(300) 10. It has been stated that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is the communication of a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing three characteristics (*trirūpa*).
If even one of these three characteristics is not stated, it is a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).

Even when [the reason] has been stated, if there is non-establishment or doubt for both the proponent and the opponent, it is because one of the three characteristics has not been stated; by the force of the word "even," this applies to two of them as well.
The semblance of a proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) means that which resembles a proof;
by the word "even" (*api*), this applies even when not explicitly stated.

When there is either non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt (*saṃdeha*) regarding either the person to be convinced (*pratipādya*) or the person who convinces (*pratipādaka*), it is a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

11. In that regard, when one of the three aspects of the reason—its presence in the subject (*dharmin*), its connection with it, or both—is unestablished or doubtful, it is the fallacious reason called "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

For example, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, its visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is unestablished for both parties. When it is to be proven that trees possess consciousness, death resulting from the removal of all bark is unestablished for the opponent.

Because he accepts that death is characterized by the cessation of consciousness, the faculties, and life-force, the probans—either "possessing origination" or "impermanence"—is unestablished for the Sāṃkhya himself when the thesis to be proven is that "pleasure and so forth are insentient. Furthermore, in this case, "possessing origination" and "impermanence" cannot be used as reasons simultaneously, but rather alternately; for the presentation of a reason is for the sake of another.

Furthermore, it is established that there is the arising of what was previously non-existent, the state of having an origin, and the destruction of what exists without remainder, which is impermanence.
Likewise, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) when there is doubt regarding its own nature or its locus;

for example, a collection of elements (*bhūtasaṃghāta*)—a mass or aggregate of the elements such as earth and so forth—is unestablished for the purpose of proving fire when it is itself doubtful whether it is actually steam or something else.
Just as in the case here: "The peacock is in this bower, because of its cry. This refers to the delusion regarding the location of its appearance.
"Appearance" (*āpāta*) means the act of appearing; "its appearance" means the arising of that cry; "the location of that" refers to the place of its arising; and "delusion" (*vibhrama*) means error.
Alternatively, "appearance" (*āpāta*) is so called because [the peacock] falls upon or comes from that [place].
That very place is the "place of arrival" (*āpātadeśa*);
it is in the confusion regarding that [place] that others say, "arrival means coming," which is incorrect.
For it is not logical that the auditory faculty functions by reaching its object,
nor is this the view of the Buddhists.
Thus, it is stated in the Abhidharmakośa:
"The eye, the ear, and the mind—these three do not reach their objects; the others are otherwise.
This [reason] is also unestablished due to the non-establishment of its locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
For example: "The self is omnipresent, because its qualities are perceived everywhere, like space."
The state of being that which has qualities such as pleasure and so forth perceived everywhere is its true nature (*tattva*).
Therefore, if this self were not omnipresent,
how could the pleasure and other states perceived in the Deccan (*dakṣiṇāpatha*) be perceived in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*)?
In the example "like space," sound is a quality of space;
and just as it is perceived in a person who is subject to transformation, so too is it perceived elsewhere.
This reason would be valid only if, for the Buddhist, the fact that the self possesses qualities perceivable everywhere were established.
As long as the self itself is not established.
Thus, the unestablished [reason] is of six kinds.
12. Likewise, when the absence of the probans from the dissimilar instances (asapakṣa) of a single property is unestablished, there is the fallacious reason called "inconclusive" (anaikāntika).

For example, when a property such as eternality is to be proven of sound, a property such as "being cognizable" (prameyatva) exists in all or part of both the similar (sapakṣa) and dissimilar (vipakṣa) instances.
In the phrase "eternality and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes [the properties of] being produced immediately after an effort and not being produced immediately after an effort.
In the phrase "knowability and so forth" (*prameyatvādika*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes impermanence (*anityatva*) and intangibility (*asparśatva*).
Of what nature is the property such as knowability that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?
It is that which exists in all or in some part of both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

In the case of "Sound is eternal because it is knowable," when eternity is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), knowability exists in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "existing in one part," here too it should be connected with "in both the similar and dissimilar instances";
this is what is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*).
Not only is "knowability" (*prameyatva*) an inconclusive fallacious reason (*anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa*) when it pervades both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*),
but also that which pervades the similar instances while occurring in only a portion of the dissimilar instances.
Likewise, that which pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) while occurring in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*),

or that which occurs in only a portion of both the similar and dissimilar instances— all such [reasons] are inconclusive fallacies (*anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa*). In this regard, the argument "sound is produced immediately after effort because it is impermanent, like a pot" is one that occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances.

Because it exists in lightning and does not exist in [the locus of] space and so forth, it indeed pervades the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), since everything that follows immediately upon effort is impermanent. For example: "Sound does not follow immediately upon effort, because it is impermanent, like lightning."
This [reason] occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣa).
Its similar instances are things that do not follow immediately upon human effort, such as lightning, space, and so forth.
Among these, impermanence exists in lightning but not in space and the like.
However, it does indeed pervade the counter-example (*vipakṣa*),
because impermanence is present in everything that follows immediately after an effort,
as in: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible, like an axe."

For "intangibility" (asparśatva) exists in one part of the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), such as cognition (buddhi) and so forth, and in one part of the similar class (sapakṣa), such as space (ākāśa) and so forth; thus, it subsists in one part of both classes.
In this way, the fourfold common inconclusive (sādhāraṇānaikāntika) reason has been described.
13. Likewise, even when there is doubt regarding this very nature [of the subject], the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For example, when it is to be proven that a certain intended person is either omniscient or possesses passion and so forth, the property such as "being a speaker" has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).
This is because an omniscient speaker is not perceived anywhere, whether in its entirety or in part.
Because such a non-perception has as its object an unobservable nature, it serves as a cause for doubt;
therefore, the exclusion of "being a speaker" and so forth from the opposite of "non-omniscience" is itself doubtful.

14. A contradictory [reason] is established by the reversal of two characteristics. Of which two? Of presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*). For example, "being produced" and "occurring immediately after an effort" are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) that are contradictory when "permanence" is the property to be proven.

The mention of two [types of contradictory reasons] is due to their distinction: one pervades the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*) while the other occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
For these two, there is the establishment of the opposite [of the intended probandum], namely, their non-existence in the *sapakṣa* and their existence in the *asapakṣa*.
These two are "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because they prove the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*).
When one of the two [forms] is unestablished and the other is doubtful, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

"Of the two" refers to positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). "When one is unestablished" means: [when either the presence or the absence of the probans in the similar instance is not established].
The absence [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) is certain,
while there is doubt regarding its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*),
as in the case: "He is free from passion, or he is omniscient, because he is a speaker."
In this case, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished and the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful.
Because both an omniscient being and one free from passion are beyond sensory perception, it is uncertain whether speech and the like exist or do not exist in them.
When there is doubt regarding these two forms [of concomitance], the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For example: "The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth.
For there is no third category other than those with a self and those without a self wherein breath and so forth could exist;
nor is there a certainty regarding their presence in either one of these two categories.

For this very reason, due to doubt regarding both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); because, consequently, there is no certainty regarding either the probandum (*sādhya*) or its opposite. Thus, when one or two of these three characteristics are unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful, there arise, as the case may be, the three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the unestablished, the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive.
Thus, by the sequence just mentioned, there are three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*):
the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
These occur among the three characteristics known as presence in the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
When one single characteristic is unestablished or doubtful;
likewise, when two or two characteristics are unestablished or doubtful—according to the case means according to what is possible.
Among these, when one characteristic consisting of the connection with the subject (*dharmī*) is unestablished, it is "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
Likewise, when the presence [of the reason] in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is unestablished or doubtful, it is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
Similarly, when each individual characteristic is unestablished or doubtful, the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*) or "inconclusive.
Likewise, when there is the establishment of the opposite of two characteristics, the fallacious reason is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*).
When there is doubt regarding the presence [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*), it is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*).
Likewise, when there is doubt regarding the presence or absence of the reason in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class, it is also indeed inconclusive.

Thus, when either of these two conditions is unestablished (*asiddha*) or doubtful in both cases, the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is either contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

16. But how is it said that there are only three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), when futility (*vaiphalya*) is also a distinct refutation of a reason? As it has been stated: "If that which is put forward as a proof in the course of a dispute is not established [as such]..."
"What is to be proven? Otherwise, would it not be undesirable, or would it simply be futile?
Regarding this, some say: "It is true that futility is indeed a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetu*).
