However, the mention of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in the *Viniścaya* and other texts is by way of classifying its lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*)."
For there are two kinds of refutation of a proof:
lack of capacity and futility.
Lack of capacity, moreover, is threefold, due to the distinctions of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikantika*).
"But futility is indeed only one [kind of fallacy].
This might be so if what is called "futility" were a refutation of the reason (*hetu*), but rather it is a refutation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This has also been stated by Uddyotakara:
"Even for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known what has already been apprehended, it would be a case of grinding what has already been ground.
This was stated by the venerable Kīrtipāda, the supreme lord of logic:
"When an action has been accomplished, [a means] that does not produce any further distinction..."
Whether it be an action, a sense organ, or some other means—why is such a thing desired? And if so, how can this be considered a refutation of the reason (*hetu*) on the grounds of its futility?
Alternatively, if it is argued that the reason is also called futile because it does not produce a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [then the following applies].
For in this way, this would not be a real refutation of the reason;
a real refutation must be stated.
Furthermore:
If the refutation of the reason's futility were distinct [from the other defects], then—
just as the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is the form of the reason that opposes "unestablishedness" (*asiddhatā*),
and positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is that which opposes "contradiction" (*viruddhatā*)— [the same would apply here].
And by means of the counteragent to inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been stated.
Likewise, by means of the counteragent to futility (*vaiyarthyapratipakṣa*), another form [of the reason] would also have to be stated;
yet no other form of the logical reason (*hetu*) is tenable.
If, then, this [point] is redundant and not a separate refutation, how is the proponent defeated by it?
17. On this point, some say that futility is indeed included within the unestablished (*asiddha*).
For instance, the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific property is sought to be known is the "thesis" (*pakṣa*).
And that property is the reason (*hetu*). Therefore, because it is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharman*), it is futile; it lapses into being unestablished (*asiddha*) right there.
But other wise ones say this:

This is not a refutation of the reason (*hetu*), but rather [it is an objection] that in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the virtues and faults of the speaker are also considered; thus, one who states what is fruitless is defeated by the very ground of "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*). For indeed, it is the subject under discussion alone—and not something irrelevant—that is the probandum (*sādhya*); this is the path that restricts the status of being a probandum to what is relevant.
By adopting this view, the enumeration [of the types of defeat] is not contradicted.

Furthermore, the defects [of a proof] are: deficiency, non-establishment, proving the opposite of the point intended by the proponent to be established, and the eighteen defects of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Regarding these, neither the objection nor the refutation has been written here for fear of excessive length. This much is established. (Ts 306)
If the refutation consists in the pointlessness of the reason, then it is included within the "unestablished" (asiddha) fallacy;
if not, then it is simply a lack of ingenuity (apratibhā).

18. Since it has been stated that the three-fold characteristic of the reason (*hetu*) alone suffices for the comprehension of the meaning, there is no separate member of proof called the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, its definition is not stated separately, as its purpose is already understood.

Although the nature of the reason—its presence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and its total exclusion from the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)—has been stated without distinction, one must nevertheless demonstrate, without further qualification, the "origination" (*janman*) and the "invariable concomitance with that alone" (*tanmātrānubandha*) for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), respectively.
The word "form" (*rūpa*) is connected with each [term].

"Existence only in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*) is this first form, which is concomitant with the probandum (*sādhya*); and "exclusion from the dissimilar class" (*asapakṣa*) in its entirety is its second form, which is the absence [of the reason] when the probandum is absent.
It has been stated:
"Without distinction" means without making [the reason] one's own nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth;
rather, they are concomitant when there is merely that [cause], namely birth (*janman*).
The compound is to be understood as "the proof has been performed.
And in demonstrating that, one should show: "Where there is smoke, there is fire," just as in the case of a kitchen and other places where fire is absent there is no smoke;

and "Where there is the state of being produced, there is impermanence," and "In the absence of impermanence, the state of being produced is impossible," just as in the case of a jar and space. Thus it should be demonstrated.
For otherwise, the presence [of the reason] in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and its absence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), in the manner described, could not be demonstrated.

The restriction to being its effect (*tatkāryatā-niyama*) constitutes the essential pervasion (*svabhāvavyāpti*) for the logical mark that is an effect (*kāryaliṅga*). "Its effect" (*tatkārya*) means the effect of that [fire, etc.]; the state of being that is "being its effect" (*tatkāryatā*).
For it cannot be shown otherwise; thus, the connection should be made by modifying the gender and number [of the words].

19. And when this meaning has been demonstrated, the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is likewise demonstrated, because it consists of nothing more than that. By this very fact, the defects of the illustrative example are also refuted.

By this very [statement], namely by the formulation of the definition of the reason (*hetu*), the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are also rejected as being means of proof, since their purpose is already understood through implication.
That which demonstrates the general and specific characteristics of the reason as they have been stated is a correct example (*saṃyagdṛṣṭānta*).
Furthermore, that in which the two characteristics [of the example] are not demonstrated is called a fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
For instance: "Sound is eternal, because it is incorporeal."
"Like action" (*karmavat*) is an example that lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*);
for in this case, the property to be proven— permanence (*nityatva*)— does not exist in action,
because action is impermanent (*anityatvāt*).
For the property of being formless exists as the probans;
because it is formless,
sound is eternal.
"In the case of the argument 'because of being formless, like an atom,' the probans is devoid of the property [of the example];
for here, the property to be proven— eternality— is present [in the atom], since the atom is eternal."
"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like a jar"—
this [example] lacks both properties, since a jar is non-eternal and corporeal.
"This person possesses passion and so forth because he speaks."
Like a man on the street.
This is an apparent example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) because its property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is doubtful.
In the case of the man on the street, the fact of speaking is ascertained by direct perception (pratyakṣa) alone; thus, the property of the means of proof (sādhanadharma) is established there.
The property to be proven, however, namely "possessing desire and so forth," is doubtful.
"This person is subject to death,
because he possesses desire and so forth, like a man on the street."

In the case of a man on the street, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—the state of being subject to death—is ascertained by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*) such as "possessing the quality of having originated" (*utpattimattva*), whereas the property of possessing passion and so forth (*rāgādimattva*) is not ascertained; thus, he is one whose probans-property is doubtful (*saṃdigdhasādhanadharmā*).
[The inference: "This man is not omniscient because he possesses passion and so forth, like a man on the street.
This is one where both properties are doubtful (*saṃdigdhobhayadharmā*).

Because it is impossible to ascertain the exclusion of both the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) from a person on the street, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Where there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the property to be proven, that is a lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), as in the case:
"Whoever is a speaker possesses passion and so forth, like a desired person."
In this case, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For there is no necessary connection between passion and the like and speech, characterized either by identity (*tādātmya*) or by origination from that (*tadutpatti*), by which there could be positive concomitance here. Thus, the positive concomitance is not demonstrated.

For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot. Although there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of being produced with impermanence, it is not expressed by the words [of the statement]; thus, it is as if non-existent.
Because the relationship of pervader and pervaded has not been demonstrated by the statement, this is a case of inverted positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*).
For example: "Whatever is impermanent is produced."

For here, when the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) "whatever is produced is impermanent" ought to be stated, one instead formulates the reversed concomitance "whatever is impermanent is produced"; all these are faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) by way of similarity (*sādharmya*).
Likewise, there are also [faults] by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), as for example: "Sound is eternal."
Because of its lack of form;
[the example] "like an atom" lacks the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyāvyatirekī*),
since the probandum is not excluded from the atom because the atom is eternal.
In this very case, the example "like action" (*karmavat*) lacks the exclusion of the probans (*sādhanāvyatirekin*),
because action is incorporeal; thus,
the probans is not excluded from the example here.
By stating "like space," it is shown that [the reason] is non-deviant from both; for both [properties] are not excluded from space,
because space is eternal and incorporeal.

Likewise, there is the fallacy of doubtful exclusion of the probandum (*saṃdigdhasādhyavyatireka*). For example: "Kapila and others are not omniscient, because they do not possess a teaching characterized by a preeminent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇātiśaya*) that would serve as a mark for their omniscience."
Here is the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta):
whoever is omniscient has taught [matters such as] astrology and so forth;
for example, Vardhamāna and others.
In the case of [the reason] "being Vardhamāna and so forth," the dual absence (*ubhayavyatireka*) of the property to be proven—namely, non-omniscience—is doubtful;
thus, it is a case of "doubtful absence" (*saṃdigdhavyatireka*).

There is also "doubtful absence of the probans" (*saṃdigdhasādhanavyatireka*), as for example: "A certain intended person is not one whose word is to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa learned in the three Vedas, because he possesses passion and so forth."
Here is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*):

"Those whose words are to be accepted are not possessed of passion and the like, such as Gautama and others, the authors of the Dharmaśāstras. In this case, the exclusion of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—namely, being possessed of passion and the like—from Gautama and others is doubtful.
The fallacy of doubtful double exclusion (*saṃdigdhobhayavyatireka*) is as follows:
"Kapila and others were not free from passion,
because they possess attachment and aversion."
Possession (*parigraha*) is the appropriation of the requisites for life;
attachment (*āgraha*) is the intense clinging to those very same things.
Here is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya):
one who is free from passion has neither grasping nor possessiveness,
as in the case of Ṛṣabha and others.

In the case of the acceptance and non-acceptance of the state of not being free from passion by Ṛṣabha and others, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) is doubtful.
An example of the lack of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*) is: "He is not free from passion because he is a speaker;
for wherever freedom from passion is absent, one is not a speaker, as in the case of a piece of stone."
Even though both [properties] are excluded from a piece of stone,
nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established through the pervasion that "every person free from passion does not speak," there is no negative concomitance;
it is a case of unshown negative concomitance (*apradarśitavyatireka*).

For example, in the formulation "sound is impermanent because it is produced, like space," one might state "like space" by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). However, although the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) exists in that case, it is not demonstrated. Likewise, when one establishes that in the absence of impermanence there is an absence of being produced—by including all possible categories of things, as in "like space"—then the negative concomitance is truly demonstrated.
It is not, however, by mere analogy that there is a reversed negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*),
such as: "Whatever is unconditioned is eternal."
For here, when it should have been said that "whatever is eternal is uncreated," he says instead that "whatever is uncreated is eternal."

21. For by means of these fallacious examples, it is not possible to demonstrate with certainty either the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the reason—namely, its presence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and its absolute absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)—or its specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). This should be connected [to the previous statement] as follows: "By means of these fallacious examples which lack the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), it is not possible to demonstrate with certainty either the general characteristic or the specific characteristic of the reason"; this is understood through the implication (*arthāpatti*) of that [statement].
It should be understood that they are to be rejected;
because by means of these fallacious examples, neither of the two types of definition can be demonstrated.
Therefore, their rejection must be seen as resulting from the implication of the facts.

22. Refutation (*dūṣaṇā*) is the statement of deficiencies and so forth. It is called *dūṣaṇā* because by means of it [the argument] is refuted (*dūṣyate*). [The suffix] *-a* is applied according to the rule *ṇyāsa-śrantho yuc*.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) [reasons] are included, as well as the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*). By this, the pointing out of those faults of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*) previously mentioned—such as deficiency (*nyūnatā*) and so forth—is intended, because it obstructs the establishment of the opponent's desired object. Furthermore, by this, one should see that the claim made by the shameless person—that only a proof of the opposite (*viparyayasādhana*) constitutes a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) and nothing else—is also refuted.
For a refutation does not consist merely in establishing the opposite,
as in the case of a contradictory [reason];
rather, it consists in obstructing the opponent's intended certainty.

Alternatively, the absence of certainty constitutes a reversal of certainty; thus, the establishment of error (viparyaya) indeed exists. However, fallacious refutations are "futile rejoinders" (jāti), while the pointing out of non-existent faults constitutes "pseudo-futile rejoinders" (jātyuttara).
The subsequent [questions] are similar by way of their genus,
because they are applied to successive positions.
Thus ends the third chapter, on Inference for Others, in the *Tarkasopāna*.
